language_wrapper: On a {rows}×{cols} wrap-around grid (a torus), Alice controls a white piece and Bob controls a black piece. Initially, the two pieces are placed uniformly at random in distinct cells. The players alternate moves with Alice going first. On any move, a player must move their piece by exactly one cell horizontally or vertically, and for each piece, the axes of motion must strictly alternate between horizontal and vertical across successive moves of that piece; on a piece’s very first move, either axis may be chosen. The torus means moving off one edge wraps to the opposite edge. Bob wins if, after one of his moves, the two pieces occupy the same cell; if this never happens, Alice wins. Let p = m/n be the probability that Bob has a winning strategy given the random initial placement (with m and n coprime). Find m.
hardness_rationale: The seed problem relies on parity and alternation constraints on a fixed rectangular grid, leading to a relatively direct invariant-based analysis. Our augmentation places the game on a toroidal grid and asks for the exact probability over all distinct initial placements that Bob has a winning strategy under perfect play. Determining this set requires solving a nontrivial alternating reachability game with state-dependent legality (HV axis alternation), turn order, and wrap-around geometry. The torus eliminates boundary traps and forces deeper analysis of phase constraints and dynamic interactions, making naive parity arguments insufficient. The correct solution employs retrograde analysis (attractor computation) on a large state graph, tracking last-axis phases and turn, and then counting initial states mapping to the winning region—substantially more intricate than the seed and not solvable by guessing.
notes: Proof sketch: Model the game as a finite directed graph of states S = {(wx,wy,bx,by,lw,lb,turn)}. Define terminal capture opportunities T to be Bob-turn states from which Bob can move onto the white piece in one step along the allowed axis. Bob’s global winning region W is the least fixpoint satisfying: (i) T ⊆ W; (ii) any Bob-turn state with a successor in W is in W; (iii) any Alice-turn state whose every successor is in W is in W. This is a standard alternating reachability (safety vs reachability) characterization for turn-based deterministic games and is correct by induction on the game tree depth. The computed W thus encodes all positions from which Bob can force capture regardless of Alice’s choices. The initial positions are Alice-turn states with both last-axis phases unspecified, which corresponds to allowing Alice’s choice of starting axis; this is handled by legal move generation from the initial state. The probability is the count of such initial states in W divided by the number of ordered distinct placements, reduced to m/n. The verifier implements this attractor algorithm over the toroidal geometry, ensuring correctness and nontriviality for generated instances.
source_question: On a \(2025\times2025\) grid table, one white piece and one black piece are randomly placed in different cells. Alice moves the white piece first, then Bob moves the black piece, and they move alternately, and the following rules are satisfied: Each move can only be one cell horizontally or vertically, and for the same piece, horizontal and vertical moves must be alternated. If after Bob's move, the black piece and the white piece exactly fall into the same cell, then Bob wins; otherwise, Alice wins. Let \(p = m/n\) be the probability that Bob has a winning strategy where \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime. Find \(m\).
